newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to set new Thomson sale terms this week.
newsitem.headline: France to set new Thomson sale terms this week.

text.p: The French government is set to unveil new terms for the privatisation of electronics group Thomson SA this week, one week after its dramatic decision to suspend the politically sensitive sale.

Official sources said on Tuesday that the new terms would be announced between now and the end of the week and industrial sources said that a statement could be due as soon as Wednesday or on Thursday, ahead of a televised interview with President Jacques Chirac that evening.
"The aim of the government is to announce new terms between now and the end of the week," an official source told Reuters.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Monday that it was a possibility the group's 58-percent stake in defence electronics group Thomson-CSF and the fully-owned consumer electronics unit Thomson Multimedia would be sold seperately.
In February, announcing the original sale plans, Chirac said the Thomson group needed to be sold as one entity.
The government announced on October 16 it had preferred an offer by Lagardere over one by Alcatel-Alsthom.
France was to have sold indebted Thomson SA for one franc to Lagardere after a 10.8 billion franc capital increase.
Lagardere would then have sold Thomson Multimedia, also for one symbolic franc, to Daewoo which promised to make investments and create thousands of new jobs in France.
But the independent seven-member Privatisation Commission said it objected to the terms of the sale to Daewoo, effectively blocking the privatisation plans.
Daewoo Electronics chairman Bae Soon-hoon is in Paris this week to seek an explanation for the rebuff and to press for an agreement under which his company can still obtain Thomson Multimedia.
Last Thursday, Thomson SA's shareholders agreed a 10.8 billion franc capital injection, exclusively subscribed by the state, which would take place before April 30.
But the European Union Commission still has to give its green light to the capital injection.

Wednesday's decision to suspend the sale was a politically embarassing U-turn for the government, already trailing at record lows in opinion polls and facing rising social unrest about early retirement at 55 after a deal with striking truckers.

It was the second privatisation to be called off in less than a month by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, after the announcement he would not sell the CIC banking unit of state insurer GAN. It added to the political problems facing Arthuis on top of the quasi nationalisation of troubled property lender Credit Foncier de France by state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC).

On Friday, trade unions fighting the state plans to wind down Credit Foncier called on Arthuis to resign, alleging a conflict of interest because of the minister's prior role at a private accounting firm which audited Credit Foncier units.

Financial analysts said that a split sale of Thomson-CSF and Thomson Multimedia made economic sense. Thomson-CSF could be sold almost immediately with an estimated market capitalisation of between 18 and 24 billion francs.
Thomson Multimedia could then receive a capital injection after agreement by the European Commission, based on a restructuring plan aimed at making profits by 1998, after which it could be sold.
Thomson SA had debts of 25.3 billion francs at the end of 1995 of which 13.8 billion were at Thomson Multimedia and 2.3 billion at profitable Thomson-CSF.
